TaoDock vs LiteLLM: Hosted Platform or Self-Hosted Gateway

Compare TaoDock and LiteLLM across hosting, provider integration, virtual keys, routing, budgets, logging and operations before choosing an AI gateway.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

The central difference

The most important difference between TaoDock and LiteLLM is not the request format. It is who operates the gateway. LiteLLM is an open-source Python SDK and proxy that gives an engineering team a unified interface across model providers. TaoDock is a hosted unified AI API platform with a model catalog, accounts, API keys, quotas, usage records and billing exposed as a ready-to-use service.

Choose LiteLLM when your team wants to own provider credentials, deployment topology and gateway policy, and is prepared to operate the supporting infrastructure. Choose TaoDock when you want to create an account and key, select from the platform's available models and let the service operator maintain the upstream connections and gateway runtime.

Both can be valid for the same organization. A platform team might run LiteLLM for internal provider access while individual users consume TaoDock for a managed catalog or desktop-client workflow. The right comparison starts with ownership and operating cost, then moves to protocols and features.

Deployment and responsibility

LiteLLM documents a library mode and a Proxy Server, also described as its LLM Gateway. In proxy mode, the operator configures model deployments, provider credentials, virtual keys, budgets, routing and integrations. The deployment can be placed inside the organization's network and connected to its database, cache, identity and observability systems.

That control is valuable when data paths, private endpoints, custom provider accounts or infrastructure policy must remain under the organization's administration. It also creates responsibility. Someone must patch the service, manage secrets, size the database and cache, monitor latency and errors, back up state, test upgrades and respond when a provider or the gateway fails.

TaoDock's public service shifts those operational duties to the TaoDock operator. The user works with the console and API instead of deploying the gateway. This is simpler for an application team, but it provides less control over the physical deployment and the upstream credentials configured behind the catalog. Check the service's privacy, support and data-handling terms if those constraints are important.

Provider and model configuration

LiteLLM's provider directory documents a large set of native, self-hosted and OpenAI-compatible integrations. The operator maps provider-specific models into gateway model names and can expose model groups to clients. That makes it suitable for organizations with existing OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, Bedrock, Vertex AI or private inference accounts that they want to normalize through one endpoint.

TaoDock users do not configure those provider adapters. They select from the models enabled by the TaoDock deployment. The public model catalog shows discoverable models and protocols, while GET /v1/models returns the exact IDs accessible to a particular API key. This reduces setup work but means the available catalog is determined by the platform rather than by each user.

If a required model or private endpoint is non-negotiable, verify its availability before evaluating convenience features. LiteLLM may be preferable when the organization must bring a specific provider account. TaoDock may be preferable when its existing catalog already covers the application and the team wants to avoid provider onboarding.

API surface and protocol translation

LiteLLM presents an OpenAI-format interface and translates requests and responses for its supported providers. Its documentation distinguishes capabilities by provider and endpoint. TaoDock also presents OpenAI-compatible endpoints and supports additional protocols where the selected model and channel advertise them.

Protocol translation is not a promise that every provider feature behaves identically. Optional parameters, tool schemas, streaming deltas, image inputs, audio, embeddings and provider-specific response fields can differ. Before choosing either gateway, define the minimum contract your application needs and run the same fixture suite against the exact model configuration.

For a conventional SDK integration, the variables are straightforward: API base URL, credential and model ID. The OpenAI SDK guide shows the TaoDock side. With LiteLLM, use the client setup documented for the proxy and the model group configured by its operator.

Routing, retries and fallback

LiteLLM documents load balancing, retries and fallbacks across deployments. Because the operator controls the model list and routing policy, it can define several provider deployments behind one client-facing model group. This is useful for capacity distribution, regional routing or failover, but the policy must be designed and monitored by the team running the gateway.

TaoDock applies routing through configured channels, priorities, model mappings and groups. Users call the model ID made available by the service; administrators manage the upstream policy. The application still needs sensible timeouts and idempotency because no gateway can make every failure safe to replay.

Test routing with failure cases. A gateway can retry a request before response bytes are returned, but a partial stream, tool execution or long-running task changes the risk. Confirm the behavior for rate limits, provider timeouts, client cancellation and partially delivered output. Record which errors the client may retry and cap the number of attempts.

Keys, budgets and access control

LiteLLM Proxy supports virtual keys and can apply budgets or limits by key, user, team and other configured scopes. The exact authentication and enterprise capabilities depend on the deployed edition and configuration. An operator must connect those controls to the organization's identity and administration process.

TaoDock exposes API-key management directly to its users. A user can create separate keys for applications and apply the expiration, quota, model and network restrictions offered by the console. The platform separately maintains the user's account balance and group access. This is convenient for individual developers, small teams and services that want application-level credentials without operating their own key service.

In both cases, do not reuse an administrator or provider credential in client applications. Issue a narrowly scoped gateway key, store it on the server, rotate it, and retain enough audit context to identify which application made a request.

Logging, cost and billing

LiteLLM can record spend and request metadata, expose an administration UI and send callbacks to observability platforms. The usefulness of those records depends on the operator's database, retention, callback and privacy configuration. Running the gateway also means reconciling its calculated costs with invoices from the underlying providers.

TaoDock records usage and consumption in the user's console and applies the platform's configured pricing and group rules. The user funds or manages the TaoDock account rather than reconciling several provider accounts. That can simplify application billing, although the platform's price and available routes may differ from direct provider contracts.

For either choice, validate cost with representative traffic. Compare recorded input, cached input, output and task units against the final charge. Do not rely on a generic tokens-per-request estimate for multimodal or dynamic task pricing.

When TaoDock fits better

TaoDock fits teams that want a working hosted endpoint, public catalog, user console and per-application key workflow without deploying an LLM gateway. It is also well suited to desktop-client integrations where a user wants to create a key, connect an application and see request records in one place.

The trade-off is dependence on the service's model catalog and policies. Confirm model availability, protocol support, quota and current pricing before building around a specific ID.

When LiteLLM fits better

LiteLLM fits platform teams that already own provider accounts, need private or regional endpoints, want detailed routing control, or must deploy the gateway inside their infrastructure. The open-source SDK can also be useful inside an application that needs a common provider interface without exposing a shared proxy.

The trade-off is operational responsibility. Budget time for security updates, dependency and configuration changes, database migrations, monitoring, backups and provider-specific regression tests. A proof of concept that starts quickly can still require substantial production work.

Migration checklist

Inventory the endpoints, parameters and models your application actually uses. On the target gateway, create a non-production key and expose only the required model. Change the base URL, key and model name in a staging environment. Run tests for ordinary responses, streaming, tools, structured output, cancellation, authentication errors, exhausted quota and provider failure.

Compare usage records and charges for the same fixtures. Check whether logs contain the identifiers your support team needs without storing secrets or sensitive prompt content unnecessarily. Finally, move a small percentage of traffic, watch latency and error distribution, and retain a rollback path until the new gateway has completed a representative billing cycle.

Frequently asked questions

Is LiteLLM a hosted model provider?

LiteLLM is an open-source SDK and gateway that connects to model providers configured by its operator. A team normally supplies provider credentials and runs or purchases the surrounding service. TaoDock exposes a hosted catalog and account experience at taodock.com.

Can an application switch between TaoDock and LiteLLM by changing the base URL?

A basic OpenAI-compatible chat integration may need only a base URL, key and model change, but production migration must also verify model IDs, supported parameters, streaming, tool calls, errors, retries and usage accounting.

Which option gives more infrastructure control?

A self-hosted LiteLLM deployment gives the operating team direct control over its gateway configuration and provider credentials. TaoDock users consume the policies and upstream catalog configured by the TaoDock platform operator.

Which option requires less gateway operations work?

Using hosted TaoDock avoids operating the gateway stack. Self-hosting LiteLLM requires deployment, upgrades, database and cache decisions, monitoring, backups and incident response, although managed LiteLLM offerings can change that trade-off.

TaoDock vs OpenRouter: Choosing a Unified AI API Gateway

Compare TaoDock and OpenRouter across model access, deployment, routing, API keys, usage records and billing to choose the right AI gateway for your team.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

The short answer

TaoDock and OpenRouter both reduce the work required to connect an application to multiple AI models, but they approach the problem from different operating models. OpenRouter is primarily a hosted model marketplace and routing service: a developer funds one account, uses one API surface, and selects from the providers and model variants available through that service. TaoDock is a unified AI API platform with a public model catalog plus account, key, quota, usage and administrative controls built around the gateway.

Choose OpenRouter when the main goal is broad hosted model discovery with provider-aware routing and a single commercial relationship. Choose TaoDock when you want the gateway experience to include end-user accounts, dedicated application keys, configurable quotas, request records and the billing behavior exposed by the TaoDock deployment. Neither choice is universally better. The deciding question is whether your team mainly needs a model marketplace or a gateway-centered application and account platform.

Product model and ownership

OpenRouter operates as a managed service. Your application sends requests to OpenRouter, and OpenRouter applies the provider selection, policies and commercial rules associated with your account and plan. Its official provider directory is useful when provider-level data handling, regional location or bring-your-own-key support influences a decision.

TaoDock also offers a hosted API at https://taodock.com/v1, but its visible product surface is broader than a model list. Users register, create separate API keys, select permitted models and groups, monitor request records and manage quota inside the same platform. For a team building on the hosted TaoDock service, that can reduce the number of separate account and usage systems needed around the model gateway.

This difference affects responsibility. A managed marketplace optimizes for choosing models and providers without running the gateway. A gateway platform with account and billing controls optimizes for connecting applications and users through the rules configured by the platform operator. Review who owns provider credentials, who sets model access and who supports downstream users before comparing individual feature checkboxes.

API compatibility and model identifiers

Both products support OpenAI-compatible requests, so a conventional integration often starts by changing the base URL, API key and model name. That similarity should not be mistaken for identical behavior. A model ID on one platform may not exist on the other, and the same model family can be backed by different provider variants, context limits or supported endpoints.

For TaoDock, request GET /v1/models with the intended API key and copy an exact returned ID. The public model catalog helps with discovery, but the key-specific model list is the operational source for an application. Then verify the endpoint advertised for that model. Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages, image generation and task-style APIs are separate capabilities; a familiar model name does not make every protocol interchangeable.

For OpenRouter, use its current model and provider documentation to select the desired route. If an application depends on provider preferences, data policies or automatic routing, reproduce those requirements explicitly rather than assuming a base URL change preserves them.

Routing and resilience

OpenRouter exposes routing choices that can select or prioritize providers for a model. Its plan page also distinguishes features such as auto-routing, preferred vendors and data-policy routing. These are important when the same model is served by several providers and the developer wants the managed platform to make provider-level decisions.

TaoDock routes through channels configured by its platform administrators. Channel priority, model mapping, availability, user groups and platform policies determine which upstream is used. From the application perspective, the stable contract is the TaoDock model ID and supported endpoint. The operational team controls the upstream configuration behind that contract.

If resilience is the reason for evaluating a gateway, test failure behavior rather than only reading a feature name. Use a staging key and confirm how each product handles provider timeouts, rate limits, streaming failures and retries. Automatic retries can help before response bytes are sent, but replaying a partially streamed or tool-executing request can create duplicate work. Your application should still use request identifiers, bounded retries and clear timeout rules.

Keys, quotas and team controls

OpenRouter plan features include workspace, budget and administrative capabilities that vary by plan. Check the live plan matrix because limits and commercial packaging can change. If you use bring-your-own keys, verify the current allowances and fees rather than relying on an old comparison article.

TaoDock users can create dedicated API keys for separate applications and apply quota, expiration, model and network restrictions offered by the console. The account balance and a key's own quota are distinct controls. This is useful when a developer wants to isolate a desktop client, backend service and experimental agent instead of sharing one credential everywhere.

Neither platform removes the need for credential hygiene. Keep keys in environment variables or a server-side secret store, do not ship them in browser bundles, and revoke a key when it is exposed. Use a different key per application so a compromised integration can be disabled without interrupting unrelated workloads.

Usage records and billing

OpenRouter publishes its current platform plans and model prices. TaoDock publishes model prices and shows the request consumption recorded for the user's account. In both cases, model price is only one part of the bill: provider route, cache behavior, input and output size, image or task units, account group and product plan can affect the final amount.

Do not select a gateway from a copied price table. Compare the live price for the exact model and route on the day of testing. Send representative prompts, record token or task usage, and reconcile the resulting charge with the platform's request record. That exercise also exposes differences in token accounting, cache reporting and error charging that a marketing table cannot capture.

TaoDock's account-oriented logs are particularly relevant when individual users or applications need their own keys and quotas. OpenRouter's activity and export capabilities may be a better fit when the team wants provider-marketplace analytics within the OpenRouter workspace. Evaluate the retention and export behavior required by your support and finance processes.

Decision matrix

Decision area TaoDock OpenRouter Question to ask
Operating model Hosted unified gateway with user, key, quota and billing surfaces Managed model marketplace and router Do you need a model marketplace, an account platform, or both?
Model discovery Public catalog plus key-specific /v1/models Hosted model and provider directories Which exact IDs and endpoints does the application require?
Provider control Controlled by TaoDock channel configuration Provider and routing options exposed by OpenRouter Who should own provider selection and policy?
Credentials Dedicated TaoDock application keys OpenRouter keys and plan-dependent BYOK options How will keys be separated, rotated and revoked?
Usage control Account balance, key quota and platform group rules Plan-dependent budgets and workspace controls Where must spend limits be enforced?
Operations Request logs and platform administration Managed service activity and provider routing Which team investigates failures and billing questions?

When TaoDock is the stronger fit

TaoDock is a strong candidate when the desired outcome includes an end-user console, application-specific API keys, quota controls, request records and a catalog governed by the platform operator. It also fits users who want to connect supported desktop clients or the OpenAI SDK to the same account and then review usage in one console.

It is not enough to say that TaoDock supports many upstreams. The practical advantage appears when the configured catalog, model groups and account controls match the organization using the service. Confirm the available models and protocols with a real key before committing an application.

When OpenRouter is the stronger fit

OpenRouter is a strong candidate when a developer wants a managed marketplace with extensive model and provider discovery, provider-level routing options and a single hosted API account. Teams that do not want to operate gateway infrastructure or build their own provider-selection layer can value that specialization.

Its commercial and administrative features differ by plan, so review the current official matrix. Provider data policies also matter: select providers and routing settings that satisfy the application's privacy, regional and retention requirements.

A safe migration test

Create a dedicated non-production key on the target platform. List models available to that key, choose the exact replacement ID and update only the base URL, credential and model configuration in a staging environment. Run a short non-streaming request, a streaming request, a tool call if used, and a realistic long prompt. Confirm the response shape, latency, usage record and charge.

Next, test an unavailable model, invalid key, exhausted quota, provider timeout and client cancellation. Record which errors are safe to retry. Only then move production traffic gradually, retaining the previous configuration long enough to compare logs and roll back. This process is more reliable than treating OpenAI compatibility as proof of identical runtime behavior.

Frequently asked questions

Is TaoDock an OpenRouter drop-in replacement?

Both expose OpenAI-compatible model access, but model IDs, supported endpoints, account controls and provider behavior differ. Treat a move as a short migration: list the models available to the new key, update the base URL and model ID, then verify streaming, tools and billing with real requests.

Which platform is easier for a small application?

OpenRouter is attractive when the priority is immediate access to a broad hosted marketplace. TaoDock is attractive when the application also needs TaoDock account quotas, dedicated keys, request records and the platform's configured routing and billing controls.

Can I compare prices from this page?

Use each platform's live pricing page. Model availability, provider selection, platform plans and group rules can change, so this guide deliberately avoids copying volatile prices into a permanent comparison table.

Do both work with the OpenAI SDK?

Both document OpenAI-compatible access. Compatibility is endpoint- and model-specific, so verify the exact API path, streaming format, tool support and model ID required by your application.

TaoDock vs Portkey: AI Model Access or Enterprise Control

Compare TaoDock with Portkey across unified model access, routing, observability, guardrails, governance, API keys, billing and deployment priorities.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Start with the job to be done

TaoDock and Portkey both sit between applications and AI models, but their primary jobs are different. TaoDock provides unified model access together with user registration, API keys, quotas, request records and platform billing. Portkey presents an enterprise-oriented AI gateway and control plane with routing, observability, guardrails, key management and governance capabilities.

As of this page's review date, the official Portkey gateway page says the product is now PRISMA AIRS AI Gateway. This guide keeps the familiar Portkey name because it remains the comparison query and appears throughout existing integrations, while current packaging and commercial details should be checked on the official page.

That distinction matters more than a raw feature count. A developer who wants one account and key for available chat, image, audio or task models has a different problem from a platform team standardizing how hundreds of applications call provider accounts under shared security and observability policies.

Choose TaoDock when the public model catalog and account workflow are the product you need. Evaluate Portkey when the organization already has model providers and needs a production control layer around traffic, safety, policy and operations. Some architectures can use both layers, but every additional gateway adds latency, failure modes and another place to investigate billing.

Product scope

TaoDock exposes a model square, console and API. Users create credentials, see the models and protocols available to their group, send requests and review consumption. Platform administrators configure upstream channels, mappings, priorities, user groups and pricing. The hosted user consumes that configured service rather than assembling providers independently.

Portkey's official material positions its gateway as part of a production stack that includes observability, guardrails, governance and prompt-related workflows. It documents routing features such as fallbacks, retries, load balancing and conditional routing, plus key management and caching. Its current branding and packaging may change, so use the official site when evaluating plans or enterprise deployment choices.

The result is a different center of gravity. TaoDock centers the model-access account and billing experience. Portkey centers the platform controls applied to model and agent traffic. Compare only the capabilities required by your workload; buying a larger control plane does not automatically improve a simple integration.

Model access and provider ownership

With TaoDock, the platform operator selects and configures upstream channels. The user sees the resulting catalog and obtains model IDs from the public pricing page or the key-specific /v1/models endpoint. This reduces provider onboarding for the user but limits choices to what the service exposes.

Portkey is typically configured in front of provider accounts or custom model hosts selected by the organization. Its value is applying a common gateway configuration to those targets. That is useful when the company already has commercial agreements, private endpoints or region-specific deployments that must remain under its control.

Ask who owns the provider relationship. If the answer is the end user who wants a ready-made catalog, TaoDock aligns naturally. If the answer is a central platform team that must govern its own provider accounts, Portkey's operating model may be closer.

Routing and reliability

Portkey documents conditional routing, fallbacks, automatic retries and load balancing. These controls are designed for teams that want gateway-level policies across provider targets. Caching and batching can also change cost and latency characteristics when they are suitable for the request pattern.

TaoDock routes through configured channel priorities and model mappings. An application uses the public model ID while the service determines the eligible upstream channel. This hides provider configuration from the user and lets the operator change routing without requiring every client to adopt a new provider SDK.

Both approaches need workload-specific testing. A retry is safe only when the request has not produced irreversible effects or partial output. Semantic caching is appropriate only when response reuse is valid for the prompt, user and policy context. Conditional routing must not send restricted data to an ineligible region or provider. Write these constraints before configuring either gateway.

Observability and request records

Portkey emphasizes detailed observability for production AI traffic, including metrics and traces used to diagnose latency, errors, cost and model behavior. Its enterprise positioning is relevant when platform and security teams require centralized investigation across many applications.

TaoDock provides request and usage logs tied to the user's account and API keys. These records help a developer confirm which model was called, how usage was calculated and what consumption was recorded. They support the operational workflow of the hosted platform but should not be assumed to provide every trace, evaluation or export feature of a dedicated observability product.

Define the questions your team must answer during an incident. If it only needs to find a failed request, status, model and charge, TaoDock's records may be sufficient. If it needs distributed traces across agents, prompts, guardrail decisions and downstream tools, evaluate Portkey's current observability features and any external integrations.

Guardrails and governance

Portkey documents input and output guardrails, including controls intended for prompt injection, sensitive information and policy enforcement. It also presents organization-wide governance features. These are meaningful for regulated or large-scale deployments, but they must be configured, tested and monitored; the presence of a catalog of guardrails is not proof that every risk is handled.

TaoDock should be evaluated primarily as the model access, account and billing gateway described by its current product. Request policies and access restrictions can reduce exposure, but do not market them as equivalent to a dedicated enterprise guardrail suite without verifying the exact control.

If guardrails are mandatory, create a requirements matrix with the protected data, enforcement point, failure action, logging requirement and bypass tests. Run adversarial and false-positive cases against the chosen product. Keep application-level authorization and data minimization even when a gateway performs content checks.

Keys, users and billing

TaoDock exposes self-service user accounts and dedicated API keys. Keys can carry the quota, expiration, model and network restrictions available in the console. Users operate against a TaoDock balance and the pricing rules shown by the platform. This model is convenient when the gateway must also function as a service portal.

Portkey documents virtual keys and centralized provider-key management. These controls are aimed at organizations distributing access to applications and teams while keeping provider secrets out of application code. Commercial plans and enterprise identity features should be checked directly because packaging changes.

The billing workflows also differ. TaoDock settles usage under its platform pricing. A Portkey deployment may track cost while the organization remains responsible for provider invoices and its Portkey plan. Compare the complete cost of service, including provider spend, gateway fees, operational staff, observability retention and support.

When TaoDock is the clearer choice

TaoDock is the clearer choice when a user wants to sign up, create a key and call models from an existing catalog without bringing provider accounts or operating a gateway control plane. It also fits service scenarios that need user quotas, platform billing and straightforward client integrations.

Confirm that the available model, endpoint and service terms meet the application. A simpler product is valuable only when it covers the required contract.

When Portkey is the clearer choice

Portkey is the clearer choice when an organization is building a central AI platform across existing provider accounts and needs advanced routing, observability, guardrails or enterprise governance. The additional product surface is justified when those controls are required across many teams and workloads.

Treat enterprise claims as inputs to a proof of concept. Verify data residency, identity integration, failure behavior, guardrail enforcement, export, retention and support in the exact plan under consideration.

Migration and layered architectures

For a migration, inventory the current model endpoints, provider credentials, routing policies, safety controls, logs and billing responsibilities. Recreate the smallest viable configuration on the target. Use non-production keys and sanitized prompts, then test ordinary responses, streams, tools, errors, timeouts and policy failures.

For a layered architecture, document which gateway authenticates the application, which one owns retries and routing, which one records the authoritative usage and how request IDs cross the boundary. Avoid enabling retries or caching independently at both layers without understanding duplication. Measure the added latency and define a single incident owner before moving production traffic.

Are TaoDock and Portkey designed for the same buyer?

They overlap at the AI gateway layer, but their emphasis differs. TaoDock combines model access with user accounts, keys, quotas and billing. Portkey emphasizes production gateway controls, observability, guardrails and enterprise governance.

Do not assume so. TaoDock provides request records and gateway controls, while Portkey documents a broader guardrail and observability product surface. List each required control and verify it in the current product before migrating.

Can Portkey route to a TaoDock-compatible endpoint?

TaoDock vs Requesty: Comparing Hosted AI Model Routers

Compare TaoDock and Requesty across hosted model access, routing, caching, bring-your-own keys, analytics, quotas, billing and integration workflow.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Two hosted routes to a unified API

TaoDock and Requesty both offer a hosted path from an application to multiple AI models. A developer can use a common API shape instead of maintaining a separate provider SDK and credential for every model family. The similarities make them easy to place in the same shortlist, but their operating and billing choices deserve a closer look.

Requesty presents itself as a model router with fallback, caching, analytics, load balancing, bring-your-own keys and a unified bill. TaoDock presents a unified gateway with a public model catalog, user accounts, application keys, quotas, request records and platform billing. The right option depends on whether provider-level routing and BYOK are central requirements or whether the account-and-catalog experience is the main need.

Use this guide to frame a proof of concept. Do not choose from a copied provider count or price claim; both products can change their catalog and commercial terms after publication.

Account and provider model

TaoDock users create an account on the platform, fund or manage quota, create one or more API keys and call the models available to their group. Upstream channels and provider credentials are configured by the TaoDock operator. The user works with the resulting catalog and pricing rather than connecting each provider account.

Requesty documents both unified access and bring-your-own-key behavior. BYOK matters when an organization wants to retain provider discounts, committed use, data agreements or direct account ownership while adding a routing layer. It also creates a two-party operational model: the team must understand which failures or charges belong to the provider account and which belong to the router.

Ask whether the application needs its own provider contracts. If not, a platform catalog and unified account can be simpler. If yes, confirm every required provider and feature is supported by the BYOK path, and verify how provider credentials are stored, rotated and scoped.

Models and API compatibility

Both services document OpenAI-compatible usage. For a basic chat application, migration often changes three values: base URL, API key and model name. Production compatibility requires more evidence. Model identifiers differ, and a model exposed by one platform can use a different provider route or parameter set on the other.

On TaoDock, use GET /v1/models with the intended key and copy an exact ID. Check the model details for supported endpoints and current pricing. On Requesty, use its current model documentation and the model names available to the account. Then run the same requests through both services.

Include non-streaming and streaming chat, tools, structured outputs, image or audio input if applicable, cancellation and error fixtures. An OpenAI-compatible response shape does not guarantee identical optional fields, token accounting or provider extensions.

Routing, fallback and load balancing

Requesty documents automatic fallback and load balancing across providers, including routing based on factors such as cost, latency or configured weights. This is attractive when the application wants the managed router to choose among several targets and continue through some provider failures.

TaoDock routes through the channel priorities, model mappings and groups configured by the platform. The application calls a TaoDock model ID, and the operator controls eligible upstream paths. Users generally do not define per-request provider routing through the public console.

For either service, test failure semantics. A fallback from one provider to another may change response style, context limits or supported tools even if the public model name appears equivalent. A retry after partial streaming can duplicate tokens or actions. Define acceptable substitutes and safe retry points before enabling automatic behavior.

Caching and response reuse

Requesty highlights automatic caching as a cost and latency feature. Caching can be valuable for repeated, deterministic prompts, but it needs clear isolation and freshness rules. Ask how keys, users, organizations, model parameters and system prompts affect the cache key. Verify expiry, bypass behavior, reporting and whether cached responses receive the same policy checks as fresh responses.

TaoDock model pricing can include provider cache behavior where supported, and request logs can report relevant usage, but that is different from assuming an application-level semantic response cache. Consult the exact model and gateway behavior rather than applying Requesty's caching claim to TaoDock.

Do not cache personalized, sensitive or time-dependent output solely to reduce cost. If caching is required, include it in the threat model and functional tests.

Keys, quotas and access

TaoDock exposes self-service API-key controls. A user can create a key per application and apply supported expiration, quota, model and IP restrictions. The key quota is separate from the overall account balance, allowing a limited credential for a desktop client or experiment.

Requesty documents API keys, groups and organization management capabilities. Evaluate how those controls map to your team structure and plan. If BYOK is used, also restrict the underlying provider credential so a compromise of the router configuration does not grant broader access than necessary.

Both services should receive server-side credentials, not keys embedded in public frontend code. Keep a rotation process and attach a non-secret application identifier to logs so the team can trace usage without recording the key itself.

Analytics, usage and billing

Requesty documents spend, latency and error analytics by dimensions such as key, user, model or project. It also states that hosted usage is billed without a token markup and that BYOK retains provider pricing; verify the current official terms and any plan fees at the time of purchase.

TaoDock records request usage and consumption under its configured model prices and group rules. Users can compare the public catalog with the charge recorded for a real request. This creates a single platform balance and support path, but it is not the same commercial model as bringing a provider account.

Compare total cost rather than one token price. Include router plan fees, provider commitments, cache hit behavior, failed-request policy, support and the engineering time required to reconcile invoices. Use representative prompts and record actual charges from both systems.

When TaoDock fits better

TaoDock fits when the desired workflow is to register, create a dedicated key, choose from an existing catalog and manage quota and request records without connecting provider accounts. It is especially direct for supported desktop clients and small applications that value one console.

Verify that the catalog contains the required model and endpoint. A unified platform is useful only when its available routes meet the workload.

When Requesty fits better

Requesty fits when managed fallback, load balancing, caching, detailed analytics or bring-your-own provider accounts are central to the architecture. Teams with provider commitments may value retaining those relationships while adding a shared router.

Validate each feature in the intended plan and region. Test cache isolation, provider failover, BYOK errors and the attribution of usage between Requesty and the provider invoice.

Migration test plan

Create isolated staging keys. List models on each platform and choose an exact mapping rather than assuming names are portable. Run a fixed set of sanitized prompts and record response shape, time to first token, total latency, usage and charge. Include repeated prompts only if caching is part of the evaluation.

Then inject failures: invalid credentials, unavailable models, quota exhaustion, provider timeouts, cancelled streams and unsupported tools. Confirm which layer returns the error and whether any retry or fallback occurred. Move production traffic gradually and keep a rollback configuration until logs and billing have been reconciled.

Frequently asked questions

Are TaoDock and Requesty both managed services?

Both provide hosted API access, but their account models and feature emphasis differ. Requesty documents routing, caching, analytics and bring-your-own keys, while TaoDock combines its configured catalog with user keys, quotas, request logs and platform billing.

Does Requesty use the same model IDs as TaoDock?

Do not assume so. List the models available to the intended key on each platform and update the application's model configuration during migration.

Which platform should I use for provider-owned discounts?

Requesty documents bring-your-own-key support for using provider accounts. TaoDock users normally consume the pricing and upstream routes configured by TaoDock. Verify current commercial terms on both services before deciding.

How should I compare automatic caching?

Test it with prompts that are safe to reuse and confirm cache scope, isolation, expiry, reporting and pricing. Never assume a cache is appropriate for user-specific, sensitive or rapidly changing responses.

TaoDock vs SiliconFlow: Aggregated Gateway or Inference Cloud

Compare TaoDock and SiliconFlow across provider aggregation, first-party inference, OpenAI-compatible APIs, model coverage, account controls, pricing and deployment.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Different layers of the AI API stack

TaoDock and SiliconFlow can both supply an API key and an OpenAI-compatible base URL, but they occupy different layers. SiliconFlow is an inference cloud and model API platform. Its official overview describes language, speech, image, video and vector capabilities, as well as reserved instances, inference acceleration and private deployment. TaoDock is a unified API gateway that connects configured upstream channels and adds user accounts, keys, quotas, logs and billing around the resulting catalog.

Choose SiliconFlow when the primary requirement is direct access to models served by its inference platform or a SiliconFlow deployment product. Choose TaoDock when the goal is a gateway account that can aggregate models from different upstream types and present them through common user and billing controls.

The products can also appear in the same architecture: a TaoDock operator may configure a SiliconFlow channel, while applications call the TaoDock model ID. In that case, understand which layer is authoritative for credentials, retries, usage and support.

Provider aggregation versus inference service

SiliconFlow develops and operates inference infrastructure. Users select from the models and modalities offered by its platform, and enterprise customers can evaluate dedicated or private deployment options. The provider relationship is direct: SiliconFlow is the service delivering the model API.

TaoDock aggregates upstream channels selected by the platform operator. Those channels can represent commercial model APIs, cloud services, self-hosted endpoints and other compatible gateways. Users do not manage every upstream credential; they consume the catalog published by TaoDock.

This distinction changes the reason to buy. Direct inference is attractive when a specific hosted model, price, latency or deployment option is the priority. Aggregation is attractive when an application wants one account and credential across several upstream ecosystems, with consistent user and quota management.

Model and modality coverage

SiliconFlow's official materials describe language, image, video, speech and vector models. Its current global and regional catalogs may differ, and models can be added, renamed or retired. Review the correct regional endpoint and live catalog for the account that will run production traffic.

TaoDock also exposes several protocol families, but availability depends on the configured model and channel. A model shown in the public model catalog should be checked against the exact endpoint it advertises. The key-specific /v1/models response is the practical list an application can call.

Do not compare only the number of models. Identify the exact text, image, audio, video or embedding workload, required context length, tool behavior, output format and region. A shorter catalog that covers the tested workload can be more useful than a larger list without the required protocol.

API compatibility

SiliconFlow documents OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible conversation protocols for supported services. TaoDock exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints and other protocols where its channels implement them. A basic SDK integration often uses the same client library with a different base URL and API key.

Compatibility still varies by model. Optional sampling fields, reasoning output, tool schemas, image input, streaming events and usage fields can differ. Model IDs are service-specific. For example, an ID with a provider prefix on SiliconFlow may map to a different public name on TaoDock, or may not be available at all.

Use contract tests. List models, send a minimal chat, stream a response, call one harmless tool, test structured output and exercise the maximum prompt shape the application expects. Preserve raw error status and request IDs for debugging, but never log credentials.

Routing and operational control

With SiliconFlow, routing inside the inference service is generally part of the provider's platform. The customer chooses the model or deployment product and consumes the resulting endpoint. Enterprise products may provide additional capacity and deployment controls; verify them in the current agreement.

With TaoDock, gateway administrators configure channels, priorities, model mappings and groups. The public model name can remain stable while the operator changes eligible upstreams. This separation is useful when the platform wants to manage provider diversity or expose different service groups to users.

If TaoDock routes to SiliconFlow, avoid ambiguous ownership. Decide whether TaoDock or the client retries failures, which service's request ID is retained, where model deprecations are communicated and which usage record is authoritative. Duplicate retry policies can multiply cost or side effects.

Accounts, keys and quota

SiliconFlow users create platform API keys and consume the balance or commercial plan associated with that service. Spending limits and enterprise controls should be verified in the relevant regional product.

TaoDock users can create separate keys for applications and apply supported quota, expiration, model and network restrictions. The user's overall balance and the individual key quota are separate. This is valuable when the same account connects a desktop client, an agent and a backend service that should not share one unrestricted credential.

In a layered TaoDock-to-SiliconFlow deployment, the application should receive only the TaoDock key. The upstream SiliconFlow credential belongs in the protected channel configuration, not in user code. Rotate both layers according to their different exposure and ownership.

Pricing and usage records

SiliconFlow publishes live prices for the models and modalities offered by its service. TaoDock publishes the prices applied to its public catalog and records consumption for user requests. The prices should not be expected to match: TaoDock's route, group and platform rules can differ from a direct SiliconFlow account.

Compare a complete workload. Text models may charge input, cached input and output separately. Image, video and audio models can use per-output, duration, character or task units. Request parameters can change the billable quantity. Send representative requests and reconcile both the returned usage and the account charge.

Avoid permanently embedding model prices in application logic. Retrieve or review current catalog information and set budget alerts with enough margin for model and traffic changes.

When TaoDock is the stronger fit

TaoDock is stronger when the application wants one account and API key across a catalog assembled from multiple upstream types, with self-service key limits and platform request records. It also simplifies supported client integrations because the same credential can be used across tools without exposing provider keys.

The limitation is that users depend on TaoDock's configured catalog and routes. Verify model availability, current pricing and protocol support for the exact key.

When SiliconFlow is the stronger fit

SiliconFlow is stronger when its inference catalog, serving performance, direct pricing, reserved capacity or private deployment options are the primary requirements. A team that only needs SiliconFlow models may not benefit from an additional aggregation layer.

The limitation is provider concentration. If the application later needs models or account controls outside the SiliconFlow platform, it may add another provider integration or gateway.

Migration and layered deployment

To migrate, map each production model to an exact target ID and endpoint. Change the base URL, key and model only in a staging environment. Test streaming, tools, multimodal input, errors, cancellation and usage. Compare latency and charges with enough requests to capture normal variation.

For a layered deployment, use a restricted TaoDock key for the application and a protected SiliconFlow credential in the channel. Propagate non-secret request identifiers, define one retry owner and monitor both usage records during rollout. Document how a SiliconFlow model retirement or regional outage is reflected in the TaoDock catalog and communicated to users.

Frequently asked questions

Is SiliconFlow an AI gateway like TaoDock?

SiliconFlow is primarily an inference cloud and model API platform with its own serving infrastructure and deployment products. TaoDock is a gateway that aggregates configured upstream channels and adds user, key, quota and billing controls.

Can the same OpenAI SDK code call both services?

A basic integration can often switch by changing the base URL, key and model ID. Verify each model's endpoint, supported parameters, streaming, tools and error behavior before treating the services as interchangeable.

Which is better for open-weight model inference?

SiliconFlow focuses directly on serving and deploying many open-weight models. TaoDock may expose SiliconFlow or other providers through its configured channels. Choose based on the exact model, route, region, price and operational ownership required.

Should I copy prices from a comparison article?

No. Both catalogs can change. Use the live pricing pages and reconcile the charge from representative requests on the day you evaluate the services.

TaoDock AI API Frequently Asked Questions

Answers about TaoDock accounts, API keys, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, models, quota, security, client setup, and common request errors.

Updated 2026-11-04

Accounts and access

TaoDock separates account access from API credentials. Sign in to manage keys, models, quota, and request records. Applications should use dedicated API keys instead of browser session credentials. A key can be narrowed to the models and usage appropriate for one workload, making it safer to rotate or revoke without disrupting unrelated systems.

Store credentials in a secret manager or controlled client configuration. Never commit a key, place it in a public browser bundle, or copy it into screenshots and issue reports. If exposure is possible, revoke the key and replace it.

Models, protocols, and usage

The live model list is the authority for what a particular key can access. OpenAI compatibility makes common clients and SDKs easier to configure, but capabilities still vary by endpoint, model, channel, and request fields. Validate ordinary responses, streaming, errors, and every advanced feature your application relies on.

Quota and pricing are operational settings rather than permanent tutorial facts. Check current pricing and the actual usage record for a request. Give development, staging, production, and independent clients separate keys so limits and activity remain understandable.

Diagnosing a request

Begin with the smallest non-streaming text request using an exact model ID. Confirm the base URL, key status, permissions, and quota. Then add streaming, tools, images, files, or other optional fields one at a time. This sequence reveals whether the problem is connectivity, authentication, model access, or a particular feature.

When requesting support, provide non-secret context: time, endpoint, model, status, request identifier, client version, and sanitized error. Remove keys, authorization headers, private prompt content, and personal data.

Frequently asked questions

How do I create a TaoDock account?

Open the sign-up page, complete the required registration and verification steps, then sign in. Registration availability and methods may depend on the current deployment settings.

Where do I create a TaoDock API key?

After signing in, open the API keys area and create a key. Give each application or environment its own key so permissions, quota, rotation, and revocation can be managed independently.

Can I recover the full value of an API key later?

Treat the value shown at creation as a secret and store it securely. If a usable key value is lost or exposed, revoke it and create a replacement instead of sharing or logging it.

What base URL should OpenAI-compatible clients use?

Most clients and SDKs should use https://taodock.com/v1. Some client presets, such as a host-oriented New API preset, may require https://taodock.com instead; follow the client-specific integration guide.

How do I find the correct model ID?

Use TaoDock's model page or call the /v1/models endpoint with the same API key. Copy the exact API ID returned to that key rather than guessing from a display name.

Does TaoDock support every OpenAI API endpoint and parameter?

No universal compatibility claim applies to every endpoint, field, model, and upstream provider. Check the API guide and test the exact endpoint, model, and optional parameters your application uses.

Why can my key see one model but not another?

Model visibility can depend on key restrictions, user group, configured channels, model availability, and deployment policy. Compare the key's permissions with the live model list.

What is the difference between account balance and key quota?

Account resources apply to the account, while a key can have a narrower usage limit. A request may be rejected by the key's limit even when the account still has available balance.

How are request charges determined?

Charges depend on the selected model, usage, pricing configuration, and applicable billing rules. Review the current pricing page and the request's usage record rather than relying on a permanent value in a tutorial.

What does a 401 error mean?

The API key is normally missing, invalid, disabled, expired, or sent to the wrong service. Recheck the Authorization value and base URL, and rotate the key if it may have been exposed.

What should I check for a 404 response?

Confirm the base URL and operation path, then verify the exact model ID. Avoid adding /v1 or a resource path twice when a client already appends it.

Why am I receiving a 429 or quota error?

Inspect whether the response represents rate limiting, account resources, or a key-level quota. Do not retry indefinitely; correct the limit or use bounded retries only for transient rate conditions.

Why does streaming work on one network but not another?

VPNs, reverse proxies, antivirus inspection, and corporate networks can buffer or terminate event streams. Compare a non-streaming request and a direct network before changing model or gateway settings.

Why do tools, images, or files fail when text chat works?

Basic chat compatibility does not prove advanced feature support. Confirm the exact model and channel support the request format and capability, then test the smallest feature-specific request.

Is it safe to put a TaoDock key in browser JavaScript?

No. Code delivered to a public browser exposes the key to visitors. Keep the key in a trusted backend or controlled local client and have the browser call your authenticated server.

Should a team share one API key?

Prefer separate keys per application, environment, team, or user boundary. Separate credentials improve least privilege, usage attribution, rotation, incident containment, and revocation.

Which desktop and self-hosted clients can connect to TaoDock?

OpenAI-compatible clients can often connect by changing their base URL, key, and model. TaoDock publishes guides for Cherry Studio, WorkBuddy, Open WebUI, AionUi, DeepChat, and SDK integrations.

What information should I include when troubleshooting a failed request?

Share the timestamp, endpoint, model, status, non-secret request identifier, client version, and a sanitized error. Never share API keys, Authorization headers, passwords, private prompts, or other credentials.

Connect AionUI to TaoDock's OpenAI-Compatible API

Configure AionUI with TaoDock's API base URL and a restricted key, verify an actual model request, and diagnose connection and quota errors.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Setup steps

  1. Create a dedicated TaoDock key

    Issue a key for AionUI, restrict its model access, and set a quota that matches the device or user.

  2. Add an OpenAI-compatible provider

    Open AionUI's provider settings and add a custom OpenAI-compatible connection.

  3. Enter the TaoDock values

    Use https://taodock.com/v1 as the Base URL, paste the dedicated key, and choose an exact model ID exposed to it.

  4. Test and confirm usage

    Send a short chat from AionUI and confirm the matching model, key, status, and usage in TaoDock.

Integration overview

AionUI can use an OpenAI-compatible provider for chat and supported model capabilities. TaoDock supplies that API surface while centralizing the credential, model permissions, upstream channels, quota, and request records. The integration reduces the number of provider secrets stored in the desktop client and gives the TaoDock operator a single place to revoke access.

An OpenAI-compatible connection is a protocol starting point, not a promise that all models expose the same features. Context limits, multimodal input, tools, reasoning controls, and streaming details depend on the model and channel. Establish a working text request first and then validate each production feature independently.

Prerequisites

You need a TaoDock account with usable quota, permission to create API keys, and at least one available model. Install a current AionUI release and confirm that the device can reach TaoDock over HTTPS.

Create an API key only for this AionUI installation. Limit it to the models the user needs and apply a quota. If several people or machines use AionUI, create a distinct key for each operational boundary. Separate keys simplify revocation, rotation, investigation, and cost attribution.

Use the key to list models in TaoDock before configuring the client. Copy an exact API ID. This preliminary test proves the key can authenticate and prevents a guessed model name from obscuring an otherwise correct connection.

Configure AionUI

Open AionUI's settings and find its model provider configuration. Add a custom or OpenAI-compatible provider and set:

  • Base URL: https://taodock.com/v1
  • API key: the dedicated TaoDock key
  • Model: an exact model ID available to that key

The base URL ends at /v1. Do not append an operation such as /chat/completions; AionUI constructs that portion. Save the provider, select it for a new conversation, and keep advanced overrides at their defaults for the first test.

If AionUI allows a custom provider name, use a clear label such as TaoDock. When multiple providers expose models with similar names, the label helps prevent a test from silently using an old connection.

Verify a real request

Start a new chat and send a short deterministic prompt: Reply with exactly: AionUI connection verified. Confirm the response and then inspect TaoDock's newest request record. The record should identify the dedicated key, exact model, successful status, and plausible token usage at the matching time.

This server-side check matters because a client can retain an earlier provider or fall back to another model. Verify streaming next if it is enabled for normal use. Then test images, tools, long context, or structured output one at a time. Use sanitized input and retain non-secret request identifiers when troubleshooting.

Troubleshooting

Unauthorized or invalid API key

Recopy the key without quotes or spaces. Confirm that it is active and that AionUI is sending it to the TaoDock provider. If the credential appeared in a screenshot, terminal history, shared configuration, or issue report, revoke it and create a replacement rather than continuing to use it.

Endpoint not found

Check that the Base URL is exactly https://taodock.com/v1. A site root can lead the client to the wrong path; a full operation URL can cause the operation to be appended twice. Test the same key against /v1/models to distinguish an endpoint issue from a model issue.

Model not found

Refresh or recopy the model list using the same key. Model IDs are exact and may differ from display labels. TaoDock also needs a usable channel for the selected model and the key's group must have access. If another known model succeeds, investigate the failing model path rather than changing authentication.

Insufficient quota

Review the account balance and the limit on the AionUI key. A narrow key quota can reject a request even when the account is funded. Confirm the request was expected before increasing the limit. Do not substitute a broadly privileged key only to bypass a deliberate restriction.

Streaming stops early

Try the same prompt without streaming. If it completes, update AionUI and test another model. VPNs, reverse proxies, antivirus inspection, and corporate networks can buffer or terminate event streams. Compare with a direct network before modifying TaoDock channel routing.

Advanced features fail

Basic text compatibility does not validate every request field. Confirm that the model and channel support AionUI's particular tool, image, file, audio, or reasoning request. Reduce the case to one feature and inspect a sanitized gateway error. Unsupported client fields should be diagnosed separately from credentials and quota.

Operating the connection safely

Keep the AionUI key isolated, rotate it when device ownership changes, and revoke it when the client is no longer used. Begin with conservative quota and expand it based on observed requests. Review the TaoDock model and usage record periodically for unexpected selections or repeated errors.

For a team, document the connection owner, intended models, quota policy, and recovery procedure without storing the secret in the document. After an AionUI upgrade, rerun the deterministic prompt and one representative advanced request. Consult the official TaoDock client guide for the current screen labels and fields.

Frequently asked questions

What Base URL should AionUI use?

Use https://taodock.com/v1 for an OpenAI-compatible TaoDock connection.

How should I choose the model name in AionUI?

Fetch or copy an exact model ID available to the same TaoDock key. Do not rely on a display name or assume IDs are portable between gateways.

Does a successful text chat verify every AionUI feature?

No. Test tools, images, files, streaming, and other advanced behavior separately with the exact model you intend to use.

Connect Cherry Studio to TaoDock's OpenAI-Compatible API

Configure Cherry Studio with TaoDock, verify a real chat request, and troubleshoot API host, key, model, quota, and streaming problems.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Setup steps

  1. Create a restricted TaoDock API key

    Sign in to TaoDock, create a key for Cherry Studio, and limit its model access and quota to what this client needs.

  2. Add the New API provider

    In Cherry Studio provider settings, choose the New API preset and enter https://taodock.com as the API Host.

  3. Enter the key and synchronize models

    Paste the dedicated TaoDock key, fetch the available models, and enable only the exact model IDs returned for that key.

  4. Send and verify a real request

    Start a new chat, send a short prompt, and confirm the request and usage record in TaoDock before relying on the connection.

What this integration does

Cherry Studio can connect to services that expose an OpenAI-compatible interface. TaoDock provides that interface while placing the API key, model access, provider channels, quota, and usage records under one gateway account. The practical result is that Cherry Studio can use models made available by TaoDock without storing every upstream provider credential in the desktop client.

The compatibility layer does not mean that every model behaves identically. Model IDs, context limits, tool support, vision support, streaming behavior, and provider errors still depend on the selected model and the channel behind it. Treat the first connection as a real integration test, not only as a successful settings save.

Prerequisites

You need a TaoDock account, an active balance or quota, and permission to create an API key. The key must be allowed to use at least one model. You also need a current Cherry Studio installation with access to provider settings.

Create a separate key for this client. Give it only the models Cherry Studio needs and set a sensible quota. If the desktop is shared, managed by another person, or used for demonstrations, assume that anything pasted into its settings can be read by someone with access to that profile. Never paste an upstream provider secret when a restricted TaoDock key is sufficient.

Before configuration, open TaoDock's model list or call /v1/models with the new key. Record an exact model ID. A familiar marketing name is not necessarily the value that the API accepts.

Exact Cherry Studio configuration

Open Cherry Studio settings and go to the model provider area. Add or enable the New API provider preset. Use these values:

  • API Host: https://taodock.com
  • API Key: the dedicated TaoDock key you created
  • Model: an exact model ID returned for that key

For this preset, do not append /v1 to the API Host. Cherry Studio builds the endpoint from the host. Adding the version segment again can produce a path such as /v1/v1/... and a 404 response.

Use the provider's model synchronization or model management control to fetch available models. Enable one known model first. A short list makes initial diagnosis easier than importing every possible model at once. Save the provider, then select it in a new conversation.

Verify the connection with a real request

Send a deterministic prompt such as: Reply with exactly: TaoDock connection verified. A visible assistant response proves that Cherry Studio reached a model, but complete verification also includes the gateway record.

In TaoDock, inspect the newest request or usage log. Check that it belongs to the dedicated key, uses the intended model, records a successful status, and shows plausible token usage. Do not use or share prompt content as a support artifact if it contains private information. A request identifier, timestamp, model, status, and sanitized error are normally more useful.

Next, enable streaming if that is how the client will normally operate. Send a longer prompt and make sure text arrives progressively and completes cleanly. If you plan to use images, tools, or reasoning controls, test those capabilities individually with the exact model; an ordinary text response does not verify them.

Troubleshooting

Authentication errors

A 401 response usually means the key is missing, copied incorrectly, disabled, expired, or sent to the wrong host. Recopy the TaoDock key without surrounding spaces. Confirm that the host is HTTPS and contains no extra path. If the key may have been exposed, revoke it and create another instead of repeatedly pasting it into screenshots or chat messages.

Model not found or unavailable

A 404 or model-related error often indicates an incorrect model ID or a key that is not authorized for that model. Refresh the list in Cherry Studio and compare the selected value character for character with TaoDock. A model may also be temporarily unavailable because no usable channel is configured for it. Try another model already known to work before changing unrelated settings.

Quota or billing failures

If the request is rejected for insufficient quota, inspect both the account balance and the dedicated key's limit. A key-level limit can block requests even when the account still has funds. Verify the group and model permissions assigned to the key. Do not respond by creating an unlimited key unless that broader access is intentional.

Streaming stops or returns an empty answer

First retry with streaming disabled. If a non-streaming request succeeds, update Cherry Studio and test a different model to isolate a client, model, or provider-specific stream issue. Proxies, VPNs, and corporate inspection products can buffer or terminate event streams; test once on a direct network before changing gateway routing.

Tools or attachments do not work

OpenAI-compatible text chat is only the baseline. Confirm that the chosen model and its TaoDock channel support the exact tool, image, audio, or document behavior that Cherry Studio is sending. Review the sanitized gateway error and the model's documented capability instead of assuming that all models accept the same request fields.

Operational recommendations

Keep the key dedicated to Cherry Studio, rotate it if the device changes owners, and revoke it when the client is retired. Start with a low quota and expand it after observing real usage. For a team deployment, document the provider name, base host, allowed models, key owner, and renewal procedure without writing the secret itself.

Review logs for unexpected model selection or repeated failures. If several desktop clients use the same gateway, give each client or person a distinct key so a problem can be contained without interrupting everyone. This also makes usage attribution more reliable than sharing one credential across machines.

The official TaoDock Cherry Studio guide remains the source of truth for the current client screens. Recheck it after a major Cherry Studio update because labels and provider presets can move even when the underlying API values remain the same.

Frequently asked questions

Should the Cherry Studio API Host include /v1?

No. When using Cherry Studio's New API preset, enter https://taodock.com as the API Host. The preset constructs the API path.

Why does Cherry Studio show no models?

Confirm that the key is active and allowed to access models, then refresh the provider's model list. Copy an exact model ID from TaoDock rather than guessing one.

Can I reuse my main TaoDock key in Cherry Studio?

It can work, but a dedicated restricted key is safer and makes quota, revocation, and usage review easier for this client.

Setup steps

  1. Create a key for DeepChat

  2. Select OpenAI Completions

What the DeepChat connection provides

DeepChat can send OpenAI Completions-style requests to an OpenAI-compatible service. TaoDock acts as that service and applies the key's model permissions, quota, and configured upstream channel. It also provides request and usage records that help the operator confirm which model handled a conversation.

This arrangement avoids entering a collection of upstream provider credentials into DeepChat. It does not erase model differences. Build confidence with a basic completion, then test each feature your workflow depends on.

Prepare TaoDock

Sign in to an account with permission to create keys and confirm that it has usable quota. Create a key dedicated to DeepChat. Restrict its models and set a limit suitable for the user or device. Do not share an unlimited administrative key across desktop applications.

List the models visible to the dedicated key. Copy an exact ID for the initial connection. This step proves that authorization and model access are working before the client is involved. It also avoids confusing a model's friendly display name with its API identifier.

Install or update DeepChat and make sure the device can reach https://taodock.com securely. If it operates behind a company proxy, note that streaming traffic may be handled differently from ordinary HTTPS requests.

Configure DeepChat

Open DeepChat's provider or model settings. Select OpenAI Completions and enter:

  • Base URL: https://taodock.com/v1
  • API key: the restricted TaoDock key
  • Model: an exact model ID available to that key

When multiple OpenAI-compatible connections exist, name this configuration clearly. Confirm the active provider and model before every diagnostic prompt so an older connection cannot produce a misleading success.

Test and verify the request

Send: Reply with exactly: DeepChat connected to TaoDock. Confirm that the response matches. Then open TaoDock's request records and find the event at the same timestamp. Verify the dedicated key, model, successful status, and token usage.

A client-visible answer plus a server-side usage record establishes the complete path. Next, test the normal streaming mode with a longer prompt. If DeepChat will use tools, images, files, or long context, run a small sanitized test for each. Record request identifiers and errors, but never copy the API key into support material.

Troubleshooting

DeepChat reports an invalid key

Remove quotes, spaces, and line breaks from the copied value. Confirm that the key remains active and belongs to TaoDock. Check that the DeepChat provider is not sending it to a different saved Base URL. Rotate the key immediately if it has been disclosed.

The request path returns 404

Use https://taodock.com/v1 as the Base URL. A root URL may not point to the API, while a full operation URL can be duplicated by the client. If /v1/models works with the same key, the credential and API version are reachable and the remaining problem is likely the model or operation.

The model is unavailable

Copy the exact ID returned for the dedicated key. Ensure the key's group has permission and TaoDock has a usable channel. If another model succeeds, preserve the working base URL and key while investigating that one model. Avoid changing several settings at once.

Quota is exhausted

Inspect both account-level resources and the key's own quota. A dedicated key is supposed to enforce its narrower limit. Confirm that usage is legitimate before increasing it, and investigate repeated automatic retries if consumption is unexpected.

Streaming is blank or interrupted

Disable streaming for one request. If the full response succeeds, update DeepChat, test another model, and compare on a network without VPN or HTTP inspection. Intermediaries can buffer server-sent events or close idle connections. If non-streaming also fails, focus first on the status and sanitized gateway error.

Tools, files, or images are rejected

Verify capability support for the exact model and channel. OpenAI-compatible text completion does not guarantee every multimodal or tool schema. Reduce the request to the smallest failing feature and compare it with a direct API request using the same model and fields.

Maintenance and security

Use separate keys for separate DeepChat users or installations when practical. A compromised or retired device can then be revoked without affecting other clients. Keep quotas conservative, review unexpected models, and rotate credentials during ownership changes.

Document the Base URL, intended model IDs, key owner, quota policy, and validation prompt without recording the secret. After major client upgrades, rerun the basic prompt, streaming test, and one representative advanced feature. Use the official TaoDock DeepChat guide as the current reference for screen-specific configuration.

Frequently asked questions

Which DeepChat provider type works with TaoDock?

Select OpenAI Completions and configure it with the TaoDock OpenAI-compatible base URL and key.

What base URL should I enter?

Use https://taodock.com/v1. DeepChat appends the operation path for requests.

Why do text requests work while an advanced feature fails?

The exact model or channel may not support the advanced fields DeepChat sends. Validate tools, images, files, and other features separately.
