Self-hosted AI client integrations

Connect Open WebUI to TaoDock's OpenAI-Compatible API

Add TaoDock as an OpenAI connection in Open WebUI, test model discovery and chat, and troubleshoot credentials, permissions, quota, and streams.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Setup steps

  1. Create a key for the Open WebUI deployment

    Issue a restricted TaoDock key for this instance and decide which models and quota its users may consume.

  2. Open the connection settings

    In Open WebUI, open Admin Settings, choose Connections, and add an OpenAI-compatible connection.

  3. Enter the TaoDock connection values

    Set the OpenAI URL to https://taodock.com/v1 and provide the dedicated TaoDock API key.

  4. Discover and test models

    Refresh the model list, select an exact available model, send a test chat, and verify the corresponding TaoDock request record.

Why connect Open WebUI through TaoDock

Open WebUI provides a self-hosted interface for model conversations. TaoDock provides an OpenAI-compatible API gateway that can expose permitted models through one endpoint and one restricted key. Connecting the two lets an administrator control model access, quota, upstream channels, and usage records in TaoDock while users work in the Open WebUI interface.

The two systems still have different responsibilities. Open WebUI manages its users, conversation experience, and local deployment. TaoDock authenticates its API key, selects an available channel according to gateway configuration, and records API usage. Decide who administers each layer before production use, especially when the Open WebUI instance serves several people.

Prerequisites and access design

You need administrator access to Open WebUI and permission to create TaoDock API keys. The TaoDock account must have quota and at least one usable model. Create a dedicated key for the Open WebUI instance rather than using a personal key copied from another client.

Restrict the key to the intended models and set a quota based on the number of users and expected traffic. TaoDock sees requests under the gateway key, so a single shared connection may not provide per-user attribution by itself. Use Open WebUI's own user controls for interface access and review both systems' records when investigating activity.

List models with the dedicated key before configuration. This proves that the key is active and establishes the exact identifiers Open WebUI should receive. It also separates gateway authorization problems from client setup problems.

Configure the connection

Sign in to Open WebUI as an administrator. Open Admin Settings, choose Connections, and add an OpenAI-compatible connection. Enter:

  • OpenAI URL: https://taodock.com/v1
  • API key: the dedicated TaoDock key for this Open WebUI instance

The URL should stop at /v1. Do not append /models or /chat/completions; Open WebUI calls those operations itself. Save the connection and refresh the model list. Select one exact TaoDock model for the initial test.

If the instance already has other OpenAI-compatible connections, name the connection clearly so administrators can tell which models and errors belong to TaoDock. Avoid disabling a working connection until the new path is verified.

Test model discovery and chat

First confirm that Open WebUI displays models available to the dedicated key. If the list is empty, do not manually invent an ID as the first response; inspect the connection, key permissions, and TaoDock model list.

Start a new chat with one known model and send: Answer with exactly: Open WebUI connected to TaoDock. Confirm the response appears. In TaoDock, find the request at the same time and verify its key, model, status, and usage. This proves that the visible response used the intended gateway rather than another configured provider.

Test streaming with a longer response. Then test each production capability—tools, images, files, structured output, or reasoning controls—separately. OpenAI-compatible endpoints can accept ordinary chat while a particular model or channel does not support an advanced field. Use sanitized prompts in tests and preserve request identifiers instead of secrets.

Troubleshooting checklist

The model list is empty

Verify the URL includes /v1 and that the key is copied exactly. Call TaoDock's model endpoint using the same key. If the direct list is also empty or rejected, fix its model permissions, group, status, or quota before changing Open WebUI. If the direct list works, review Open WebUI server logs for a connection or TLS error and restart or refresh the connection as appropriate for the deployment.

Open WebUI reports unauthorized

A 401 generally means the API key is missing, invalid, disabled, or sent to the wrong endpoint. Replace the key if it may have been exposed. Remember that a secret stored in a server-side administrator connection should not be placed in browser-visible custom JavaScript or shared screenshots.

A selected model returns 404 or unavailable

Copy the exact model identifier returned to this key. Check that TaoDock has a usable channel for the model and that the key's group can access it. If several models work and one fails, treat it as a model or provider path issue rather than rebuilding the entire connection.

Requests fail for quota

Inspect the TaoDock account balance and the key-specific quota. A shared interface can consume a narrow key limit faster than a single desktop client. Increase limits intentionally and monitor usage; do not replace the key with an unrestricted administrator credential as a shortcut.

Streaming hangs behind a reverse proxy

Try non-streaming chat and a direct network route. Reverse proxies in front of either Open WebUI or the client may buffer server-sent events or apply short timeouts. Review proxy streaming and idle-timeout configuration, but keep authentication headers out of diagnostic output.

Tools, images, or files fail

Confirm capability support for the exact model and TaoDock channel. Reduce the request to the smallest failing example and compare it with an API call that uses the same fields. Some client features transform files or tool schemas before sending them, so a basic text test cannot validate those paths.

Production operations

Use separate TaoDock keys for development, staging, and production Open WebUI instances. Rotate keys through the administrator connection and verify a test request before revoking the old credential. Record the key's owner, allowed models, and quota policy without recording the secret.

Monitor repeated errors and unexpected model usage. When many Open WebUI users share one gateway credential, pair TaoDock's aggregate API record with Open WebUI's own audit or user context. Define which administrator handles client access, which handles gateway routing, and who responds when an upstream provider is unavailable.

Revisit the official TaoDock Open WebUI guide after significant client upgrades. The exact menu labels can change, while the core connection remains the TaoDock /v1 base URL plus a restricted API key.

Frequently asked questions

Where is TaoDock configured in Open WebUI?

An Open WebUI administrator adds it under Admin Settings, Connections, as an OpenAI-compatible connection.

What OpenAI URL should Open WebUI use?

Set the URL to https://taodock.com/v1 and use a dedicated TaoDock API key.

Should one key be shared by multiple Open WebUI instances?

Separate keys are recommended so each instance can have its own model permissions, quota, usage attribution, rotation, and revocation.

Developer API integrations

Use the OpenAI SDK with TaoDock's Compatible API

Point the OpenAI SDK at TaoDock, keep credentials in environment variables, verify models and chat responses, and handle common API errors safely.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Setup steps

  1. Create a least-privilege API key

    Generate a TaoDock key for this application, restrict its models and quota, and store it in TAODOCK_API_KEY.

  2. Configure the SDK client

    Initialize the OpenAI SDK with base_url or baseURL set to https://taodock.com/v1 and the environment-supplied key.

  3. List and select a model

    Query the models endpoint with the same client and use an exact model ID returned for the key.

  4. Send and reconcile a test request

    Make a small completion request, preserve its non-secret request context, and verify status, model, tokens, and usage in TaoDock.

When to use the SDK integration

An application already built around an OpenAI SDK can often connect to TaoDock by changing the base URL, API key, and model ID. TaoDock then authenticates the application key, applies its permissions and quota, routes the request through configured channels, and records usage. This is useful when an application needs access to multiple providers without embedding every upstream credential.

OpenAI compatibility reduces client changes, but it is not a guarantee that every method, request field, model feature, or error behaves identically. Validate the precise endpoints your application uses. Streaming, tools, images, audio, files, structured output, embeddings, and response APIs should each be tested with their selected model.

Prepare credentials and models

Create a TaoDock API key specifically for the application and environment. Development, staging, and production should not share one credential. Restrict model access and set quota or expiration according to the workload. Store the secret in a managed environment variable or secret store—not in source code, browser bundles, logs, screenshots, or committed .env files.

For local examples, use the variable name TAODOCK_API_KEY. The name makes it clear that this is a gateway credential rather than a direct upstream provider key. Load it through your runtime's normal environment mechanism.

Before sending a completion, use the same SDK client or a direct request to list models. Select an exact model ID returned to the key. This avoids assuming that identifiers from another gateway are portable.

Python configuration

Initialize the supported Python SDK with TaoDock's API base and the environment variable:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["TAODOCK_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://taodock.com/v1",
)

models = client.models.list()
print([model.id for model in models.data])

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="YOUR_MODEL_ID",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with exactly: SDK connected"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Replace YOUR_MODEL_ID with a value returned for the key. Do not copy a model name from a pricing article or another platform without checking the live list.

JavaScript and TypeScript configuration

Server-side JavaScript can configure the official SDK in the same way:

import OpenAI from 'openai'

const client = new OpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.TAODOCK_API_KEY,
  baseURL: 'https://taodock.com/v1',
})

const models = await client.models.list()
console.log(models.data.map((model) => model.id))

const response = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'YOUR_MODEL_ID',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Reply with exactly: SDK connected' }],
})
console.log(response.choices[0]?.message.content)

Run this only in a trusted server or local process. Shipping a TaoDock key in public browser JavaScript exposes it to every visitor. A browser application should call your authenticated backend, which holds and controls the gateway credential.

Verify more than the response text

After the test returns, find the matching request in TaoDock. Confirm the dedicated key, exact model, status, token usage, and charge or quota change. Preserve a non-secret request identifier if available so client and gateway records can be correlated.

Test failure behavior deliberately. Use a disabled test key, a nonexistent model, and an intentionally small quota in a non-production environment. Confirm that the application distinguishes authentication failures, permission or model errors, rate limits, quota exhaustion, provider failures, and timeouts. Retry only errors that are safe for the operation; uncontrolled retries can multiply cost or duplicate side effects.

For streaming, consume and close the stream according to the SDK's documented lifecycle. Test client cancellation and make sure your server stops unnecessary downstream work. For tools or structured output, validate the exact schema and model instead of inferring support from an ordinary chat completion.

Common errors

401 authentication failed

Confirm TAODOCK_API_KEY is present in the actual process environment and not only in an unopened shell or ignored file. Check for whitespace and verify that the client uses the TaoDock base URL. Revoke any key that has appeared in an exception dump or public log.

404 endpoint or model not found

The base URL is https://taodock.com/v1; the SDK appends paths. A full operation path can be duplicated. If model listing works, use one of its exact IDs and confirm the key's permissions and TaoDock channel availability.

429 or quota errors

Rate limits and quota are different conditions even when an SDK surfaces similar status handling. Inspect the sanitized response and TaoDock records. Use bounded exponential backoff only for retryable rate or transient failures. Increasing a key limit is an access decision, not a generic error-recovery step.

Timeout or upstream failure

Set explicit client timeouts appropriate for the endpoint and model. Preserve error type, status, request identifier, model, and duration while excluding prompts and secrets where possible. Define whether the application or TaoDock owns retries and fallback so both layers do not independently duplicate requests.

Unsupported parameters

Remove optional fields until the smallest request succeeds, then restore them one at a time. Optional parameters and zero values may have meaningful semantics. Consult the TaoDock API guide and the chosen model's capability rather than assuming an SDK method maps identically across providers.

Production checklist

Use separate least-privilege keys per service and environment. Keep secrets in a vault or managed runtime store, rotate them, and revoke unused credentials. Pin and test SDK upgrades. Apply request timeouts, bounded concurrency, and intentional retry rules. Monitor error distribution, latency, usage, and quota without recording authentication headers or sensitive prompt content.

Before migration, run representative non-streaming, streaming, tool, cancellation, and error fixtures. Compare response shape and usage with the previous path. Roll out gradually and keep a reversible configuration until the new gateway has handled normal traffic and failure conditions.

Frequently asked questions

Does the OpenAI SDK need a different package for TaoDock?

No. Configure the supported OpenAI SDK with TaoDock's base URL and a TaoDock API key.

What base URL should SDK code use?

Use https://taodock.com/v1 and let the SDK append resource paths.

Is every OpenAI SDK method supported for every TaoDock model?

No. Compatibility and capabilities depend on the endpoint, selected model, channel, and fields. Test the exact methods your application uses.

Desktop AI client integrations

Connect WorkBuddy to TaoDock's OpenAI-Compatible API

Set up WorkBuddy with TaoDock's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, validate an actual request, and resolve key, model, quota, and protocol issues.

Reviewed 2026-11-04 · Updated 2026-11-04

Setup steps

  1. Issue a WorkBuddy-specific API key

    Create a TaoDock key with only the model permissions and quota that WorkBuddy requires.

  2. Add a custom OpenAI-compatible provider

    Open WorkBuddy's model service settings, add a custom provider, and keep its custom protocol option disabled.

  3. Enter the endpoint and model

    Set the service URL to https://taodock.com/v1, paste the dedicated key, and use an exact model ID available to that key.

  4. Verify the request in both products

    Send a short prompt from WorkBuddy, then confirm the status, model, key, and usage in TaoDock's request records.

Integration overview

WorkBuddy can call an OpenAI-compatible service instead of connecting directly to each upstream model provider. TaoDock supplies the compatible endpoint and centralizes the API key, allowed models, quota, channels, and usage records. This keeps provider credentials out of the desktop client and gives an operator one place to revoke or restrict access.

Compatibility covers the API contract that the client uses; it does not make every model interchangeable. WorkBuddy features that depend on tools, vision, long context, structured output, or a particular streaming convention must be verified with the selected model. The safest rollout begins with a basic chat and then tests each advanced capability separately.

Before you start

Confirm that your TaoDock account can create keys and has usable quota. Create a new key specifically for WorkBuddy. Restrict its model access to the small set you intend to use and apply a quota appropriate for the device or user. A separate credential makes rotation and investigation much easier than sharing a broad key across applications.

Obtain an exact model ID from TaoDock's model list or /v1/models using that key. Model display names in a user interface may differ from the API value. If the key cannot see the model before WorkBuddy is configured, the client will not fix that authorization problem.

Use a current WorkBuddy version and make sure the device can reach https://taodock.com over TLS. Corporate proxies or VPNs sometimes interfere with streaming; knowing whether the same endpoint works with a direct request helps isolate those network conditions.

WorkBuddy settings

Open WorkBuddy's settings and locate its model service or custom provider configuration. Add an OpenAI-compatible service and enter:

  • Service URL: https://taodock.com/v1
  • API key: the dedicated TaoDock key
  • Model: an exact model ID returned by TaoDock
  • Custom protocol: disabled

The /v1 segment is required in WorkBuddy's service URL. Do not add /chat/completions; the client appends the operation path. Do not put a trailing operation path copied from a command-line example into the base field.

Save the connection and select the new provider and model for a fresh conversation. Avoid changing timeout, proxy, sampling, and advanced model settings simultaneously. A minimal configuration makes any error easier to attribute.

Validate an actual completion

Send a short instruction with a predictable result, for example: Return the words WorkBuddy connected and nothing else. Confirm that the assistant responds and that the selected provider remains TaoDock.

Then open TaoDock's request records. Find the matching timestamp and verify the key, model, successful status, and token usage. This second check catches cases where a client silently falls back to a different provider. It also confirms that quota accounting is associated with the intended credential.

Run a second test using the mode your team expects in production. If streaming is enabled, confirm that partial text arrives and the stream closes normally. If WorkBuddy uses tools or workspace context, test with sanitized content and check the gateway error details if it fails. Never include a live key in a screenshot or support transcript.

Common problems

401 unauthorized

Recopy the key and remove spaces or quotes. Make sure WorkBuddy is sending it to TaoDock rather than to a provider configuration left over from an earlier test. Check whether the TaoDock key has been disabled or expired. Rotate the credential immediately if it has appeared in logs, screen recordings, or public issue reports.

404 endpoint or model errors

The service URL must be https://taodock.com/v1, not the site root and not the full chat-completions endpoint. For a model error, list models with the same key and copy the precise ID. The model also needs a usable TaoDock channel; a catalog entry alone does not guarantee that every account or group can call it.

Insufficient quota

Review account balance, key quota, group access, and model availability. A restricted WorkBuddy key can correctly reject a request even when a broader administrator key succeeds. Increase the narrow limit only after confirming that the request is expected. Repeated retries against a quota failure create noise without resolving the cause.

Streaming or connection resets

Test a non-streaming request. If it succeeds, update WorkBuddy, try a second model, and temporarily bypass any VPN or HTTP inspection layer. Event streams can be buffered by intermediaries. If all request types fail, verify DNS and TLS access to TaoDock before changing the API protocol setting.

Feature-specific failures

A plain chat response does not prove tool calling, image input, file processing, or structured output. Confirm the selected model's capabilities and the fields WorkBuddy sends. Try the smallest feature-specific request and compare its sanitized error with a direct API request using the same model.

Safe ongoing use

Give each team, device, or automation a distinct key. That design lets you revoke one WorkBuddy installation without breaking unrelated applications. Keep key quotas conservative until the usage pattern is understood and review the TaoDock records for unexpected models or repeated failures.

When upgrading WorkBuddy, run the small verification prompt again before a broad rollout. Client updates can change provider labels or request behavior. Keep the official TaoDock WorkBuddy guide bookmarked for current screen-specific instructions, while this page provides the validation and operational checklist around those settings.

Frequently asked questions

What URL should WorkBuddy use for TaoDock?

Use https://taodock.com/v1 as the OpenAI-compatible service URL.

Should WorkBuddy's custom protocol option be enabled?

No. Follow the TaoDock guide and keep the custom protocol option disabled for this OpenAI-compatible connection.

Why does a model work in TaoDock but not WorkBuddy?

Confirm that WorkBuddy uses the exact API model ID and that the selected feature is supported by that model and channel.
